name: Chang'an
info: Chang’an was a capital of Chinese dynasties in Shaanxi from the Western Han to the Tang, in two walled cities on nearby sites, and was at times the largest city in the world; Xi’an stands there today.

facts.founded: Liu Bang, the founder of the Han dynasty, made it his capital after 202 BCE, moving his court to the Changle Palace in 200 BCE; the Sui built a new city, Daxing, in 582, which was renamed Chang’an in 618.
facts.where: In the Guanzhong region along the Wei River in Shaanxi province, China; the Han city lay about 5 km north-west of the Xi’an of the Ming and Qing, and the Sui and Tang city south-east of it.
facts.known: Capital of the Western Han, Sui and Tang; the Weiyang Palace; the Silk Road’s eastern end; a grid of walled wards and two great markets; Sogdian, Persian and other foreign communities; the model for Nara and Kyoto; the destruction of 904
facts.today: The site lies within the modern city of Xi’an, whose walls the Ming built around the former Sui and Tang palace district.

t: Chang’an was the capital of the Western Han and, after a long break, of the Sui and Tang, who built a new city to the south-east of the Han one.
Its Tang walled city held 800,000 to 1,000,000 people by modern estimates and drew merchants, pilgrims and scholars from across Asia.
The An Lushan rebellion and later sacks destroyed much of it, and in 904 Zhu Wen had it demolished and its people moved to Luoyang.
dyk: The Weiyang Palace of the Han, which served as an imperial palace for many later dynasties, covered 4.8 square kilometres, nearly seven times the area of the Forbidden City.
ev: Liu Bang moves his court to the Changle Palace
The walls of the Han city are completed
Rebels capture and sack the city and Wang Mang is killed
Emperor Wen of the Sui sites a new capital, Daxing, south-east of the ruined Han city
Daxing is renamed Chang’an when Li Yuan founds the Tang
An Lushan’s forces occupy the city
Huang Chao occupies the city and makes it the seat of his Qi dynasty
Zhu Wen orders the buildings demolished and the capital moved to Luoyang

sections.origins:
The site south of the Wei River has been inhabited since Neolithic times, when the Yangshao culture had a major centre at Banpo from about 5000 to 4300 BCE. Fenghao, the twin capitals of the Western Zhou, stood nearby from about 1064 to 771 BCE, and the Qin had their capital at Xianyang, north of the Wei, from 350 to 207 BCE. Chang’an itself was a small village under the Qin.

After the Han dynasty was established in 202 BCE its founder Liu Bang first ruled from Luoyang, as most of his advisors wished. The soldier Lou Jing and the general Zhang Liang persuaded him that the Guanzhong region, the Zhou and Qin heartland along the Wei River, could support a larger core population and was much better protected, and that Chang’an was far more central in the lands the Han emperor administered directly. His chancellor Xiao He rehabilitated the Qin Xingle Palace as the Changle Palace, completed in 200 BCE, and began to renovate the Zhangtai Palace as the Weiyang Palace. According to Sima Qian, Liu Bang reproached him for the extravagance, and Xiao He answered that the magnificence was needed to overawe rivals and affirm the dynasty’s legitimacy. Thousands of clans of the military aristocracy were relocated to the region.
sections.growth:
Chang’an had a population of 146,000 in 195 BCE, when Liu Ying, the Hui Emperor, began work on the city walls. They were finished in September 191 BCE with 146,000 to 290,000 workers serving 30-day corvees and 20,000 convicts. Emperor Wu began a third phase of building that peaked in 100 BCE with many new palaces, and in 120 BCE he turned the Shanglin Park into an imperial park again. By the end of his work two thirds of the area within the walls was taken up by imperial palaces, and nearly three quarters of China’s nobility lived in Chang’an or near it. It was a consumer city, existing for its role as the political and military centre of China rather than for manufacturing or trade. The census of 2 CE recorded 246,200 people in 80,000 households in the walled city, and 682,000 in the whole metropolitan region.

The Sui and Tang city was a different one. In 582 Emperor Wen of the Sui sited a new capital, Daxing, south-east of the much ruined Han city, and it was renamed Chang’an in 618. Around 750 Chinese records called it a “million-man city”. Most modern estimates put the population inside the Tang walls at around 800,000 to 1,000,000. The census of 742 recorded 1,960,188 people in 362,921 households for Jingzhao, the province that held the capital, and scholars including Charles Benn and Patricia Ebrey agree that the city and its hinterland could have supported about 2,000,000.
sections.rulers:
The Western Han ruled from Chang’an. Under Wang Mang’s short-lived Xin dynasty the palaces were altered towards the plans recorded in the Kaogongji. In the Lülin rebellion that ended his reign the city was captured and sacked on 4 October 23 CE, and Wang was killed two days later. The Eastern Han chose Luoyang, and Chang’an was occasionally called the Western Capital. In 190 the chancellor Dong Zhuo took the Han court there, and in 196 it moved back to Luoyang and then to Xuchang.

Chang’an was the Jin capital from 312 to 316, fell to the Han-Zhao in 316 and was then the capital of the Han-Zhao (318 to 329), the Former Qin (351 to 385) and the Later Qin (384 to 417). Under the Later Qin ruler Yao Xing it became an important hub of Buddhism in China. The Eastern Jin recovered it briefly in 417, the Helian Xia took it in 418 and the Northern Wei in 426. It was the capital of the Western Wei (535 to 557) and the Northern Zhou (557 to 581). The Sui built Daxing in 582, and the Tang, founded by Li Yuan in 618, held Chang’an until its downfall. The Weiyang Palace of the Han city served as the imperial palace of many of these dynasties, among them the Xin, the Western Jin, the Former and Later Qin and the Northern Zhou, until its destruction under the early Tang.
sections.life:
The Tang city was an irregular rectangle of wards, with eight main avenues dividing it into nine districts; the articles give about 110 walled wards in the outer city, and elsewhere speak of more than a hundred or of 160. A ward held about 50 to 100 families. The city had a Palace City for the emperor, an Imperial City for officials and an Outer City for the people. The Imperial Way, the widest street, was 150 m wide. The two official markets, the East and the West, each covered nine blocks around a central block of government offices. They opened at noon at the sound of 300 drum beats and closed about an hour and three quarters before dusk, and small night markets in the wards went on despite an attempt to close them in 841. The West Market had a Persian bazaar.

Han Chinese and Sogdians were two of the largest groups. Travellers came from India, the Arabian peninsula, the Iranian plateau and the east African coast, and some stayed. At least five or six Zoroastrian temples stood in the city, and four around the West Market. The Church of the East reached China in about 635, and Emperor Xuanzong is said to have decreed a place of worship for Muslims around 742. Emperors also restricted religions: Manichaeism was banned in 843, and Buddhism was banned and later restored. Several laws separated foreigners from Han Chinese, and in 779 an edict made the Uyghurs in the capital wear their ethnic dress. The writer Yuan Zhen called non-Chinese people barbaric and said that their ways would harm the Chinese way of life.
sections.crises:
A famine in 682, after droughts, floods, locusts and epidemics, hit both Chang’an and Luoyang. In 843 a fire destroyed 4,000 buildings in the East Market, while the wide avenues kept it from spreading across the city.

Much of the city was destroyed in the repeated sackings of the An Lushan rebellion and the events after it. An Lushan’s and Shi Siming’s forces occupied it in 756, and the Tang government and its allies retook it in 757. In 763 the Tibetan Empire briefly occupied it, and in 765 the Tibetans and the Uyghur Khaganate besieged it. Rebels occupied it again in 783 and 784.

In 881 the rebel Huang Chao occupied Chang’an and made it the seat of his Qi dynasty. The Tang regained it in 882, but its forces, though welcomed by the people, looted the city before being driven out, and Huang Chao then carried out a systematic slaughter of the inhabitants. The Tang took it again in 883. In 904 the warlord Zhu Wen ordered the buildings demolished and the materials moved to Luoyang, which became the capital. The residents and the emperor Zhaozong were forced to move there too. Chang’an never recovered.
sections.legacy:
After 904 the Youguo Governorate was established at Chang’an, and its first governor Han Jian rebuilt it around the old Imperial City. The new town, called Xincheng, was less than a sixteenth of the size of the old city, and the rest was overrun by nature and used for farming. Chang’an was of minor importance until the Northern Song. The Ming gave it the name Xi’an and built walls around the former Sui and Tang palace district, an area about an eighth the size of the medieval city at its height. Some Tang monuments still stand.

Victor Cunrui Xiong calls the Sui and Tang city the most important city of early imperial China. Its grid of walled wards completed a long tradition of planning Chinese capitals and influenced several later East Asian capitals; the Japanese modelled Heijo-kyo (Nara) and later Heian-kyo (Kyoto) on it, on a more modest scale and without the same fortifications. Archaeologists found two Sogdian tombs in Xi’an in the early 2000s, those of An Jia and Shi Wirkak, which combine Chinese and Sogdian burial customs. The Han Chang’an lay about 5 km north-west of the Ming and Qing Xi’an, though the modern city has grown to include it.

summary: Chang’an was the capital of the Western Han, and then, in a new walled city to the south-east, of the Sui and Tang, when it held 800,000 to 1,000,000 people by modern estimates. Rebellions ruined it, and in 904 Zhu Wen had it demolished. Xi’an now stands on the site.
references: Edward H. Schafer, The Golden Peaches of Samarkand: A Study of T'ang Exotics (University of California Press, 1985)
Charles Benn, China's Golden Age: Everyday Life in the Tang Dynasty (Oxford University Press, 2002)
Nancy Shatzman Steinhardt, Chinese Architecture: A History (Princeton University Press, 2019)
Alfred Schinz, The Magic Square: Cities in Ancient China (Edition Axel Menges, 1996)
Valerie Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History with Documents (Oxford University Press, 2017)
notes: START: the lead gives "from 202 BC"; the History says Liu Bang moved his court to the Changle Palace in 200 BC (completed in the 2nd month of Year 7) and started renovating in 202 BC. I used -202 as start and gave 200 BCE as the first event.

END: the lead says capital city "from 202 BC to 907 AD" while the text says Zhu Wen forced the move to Luoyang in 904 and ordered the buildings demolished; I used 904 as the end of Chang’an as a capital and did not use 907.

WARDS: the article contradicts itself: "160 walled 1x1 li wards" (City structure, apparently the Han plan), "about 110 separately walled wards, two markets" (Outer City, Tang) and "more than one hundred" (Legacy). I gave about 110 for the Tang city and mentioned that other figures are given. Also "Nine Markets" (Han) versus two Tang markets: I wrote only about the Tang two.

WALLS: the article gives two incompatible sets of dimensions for the Tang walls (5 mi by six miles, 5.5 m high, 78 km2; and a 25.7 km wall, 12 to 16 m thick). I left all wall dimensions out. The article also gives the Han walls no length.

The "City structure" section mixes Han and Tang (the Weiyang Palace under Han, the Imperial City and Palace City under Sui and Tang): I put the Palace, Imperial and Outer City only under the Tang city. The Han capital and the Tang city being different cities on nearby sites is stated by the article ("main areas of Sui and Tang-era Chang’an was south of the earlier settlement and southeast of Weiyang"; "Sui Daxing and Tang Chang’an occupied the same location").

Weiyang's area: the lead says 4.8 km2 and "nearly seven times larger than the Forbidden City", but the Palaces section gives it as a 2250x2150 m rectangle enclosing 5 km2 and the Changle Palace as 6 km2. I used the lead figure in dyk only.

Population: 800,000-1,000,000 within the Tang walls are "most modern estimates"; the 742 census figure is for Jingzhao, not the city; both hedged as the article hedges them. The Han figures (146,000 in 195 BCE, 246,200 in the AD 2 census) are as stated. The claim of "million-man city" is "around 750 AD, Chinese records".
The article says Han Chang's earlier phase "the fourth from 1 BC to AD 24 when it was destroyed"; I used the sack of 4 October AD 23 only.

The article gives the Muslim decree as "around the year 742 AD ... Emperor Xuanzong decreed ... the Great mosque of Xi'an was established where it still stands"; written with "is said to have" because the article does not source it and the mosque's date is not otherwise given. The 843 Manichaean ban and the statement that Buddhism was banned and restored are as in the text; its "emperor placed a ban on Buddhism and Christianity, and only Buddhism survived" is left out as unclear.

The Tang religion paragraph also says "crackdown on religions ... focused on Sogdian or Kuchan religions such as Islam or the Church of the East": left out (confusing). The 779 edict is as written; the article says "Uighurs".

Left out: the An Lushan rebellion's causes, the Jingyuan Rebellion beyond 783-784, the festivals, the Sogdian tomb epitaph details, water systems and food supply. The article gives no date for the end of the Tang beyond 907 in the lead; Zhaozong is named only as the emperor moved in 904.
The lead says the Weiyang Palace was destroyed "under the early Tang"; not used. Not found: the date of Han Jian's governorship, or any date for the Ming adoption of Xi'an.
